\chapter{Please: Water, Bread, Tea, Key}
\label{ch:fa-please-requests}
\hlchaptermodality{9}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can politely ask for water, bread, tea, or my key in Persian, and I can name the four vocabulary layers those four words come from.}

The chapter closes on kelid, a Greek loan, then runs all four requests back to back — âb, nân, chây, kelid, each with lotfan — and reuses the ezafe from Chapter 2 to ask for kelid-e man, my key.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[âb]{\fa{آب} — water, and Persian's first \textquotedblleft{}please\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:FA-C09-ab}



\begin{quote}
The last chapter closed on \textbf{\fa{داشتن}} \emph{dâshtan}, “to have,” stem \textbf{\fa{دار}} \emph{dâr}. This chapter names what to ask for when you do not have it yet.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\fa{آب}} — \emph{âb} — \textbf{water}
\end{quote}

Two letters, both already yours: \textbf{\fa{آ}}, alef with \emph{madde}, from \textbf{\fa{آمدن}}; then \textbf{\fa{ب}} \emph{b}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: your first Persian \textquotedblleft{}please\textquotedblright{}}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\fa{آب،} \fa{لطفاً}.} — \emph{âb, lotfan.} — \textbf{Water, please.}
\end{quote}

Name the thing you want, add \textbf{\fa{لطفاً}} \emph{lotfan}, and the request is complete — no verb required. \textbf{\fa{لطفاً}} ends in a small hooked mark, \textbf{\fa{ً}}, called \emph{tanvin}: an Arabic grammatical ending, pronounced \emph{-an}, that survives in Persian only inside a short list of frozen Arabic adverbs borrowed whole — \textbf{\fa{لطفاً}} and \textbf{\fa{تقریباً}} \emph{taghriban}, “approximately,” are two of them — and plays no part in ordinary Persian spelling. This is the first request this track has built.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\fa{آب}} continues Old Persian \emph{\textbf{āp-}}, from Indo-European *\emph{h\textsubscript{2}ep-}, “water” — the root Sanskrit kept as \textbf{áp-}, still visible today inside a place-name: \textbf{Punjab} is usually explained as this same word, \textbf{\fa{پنج} \fa{آب}} \emph{panj âb}, “five waters,” naming the region's five rivers.

Hindi and Marathi's everyday word for water, \textbf{pānī}, is not this word at all. Sanskrit holds a second, unrelated root for water too — \textbf{pā-}, “to drink,” from *\emph{peh\textsubscript{3}-}, the root hiding inside English \textbf{potion} and \textbf{poison} — and it is that second root modern Hindi and Marathi kept for everyday use. \textbf{\fa{آب}} and \textbf{pānī} are not cousins; they are two different ancient words for the same thing, and Persian happened to keep the older one.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{âb} — water
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{âb, lotfan.} — water, please
  \item \emph{Connect:} \textbf{âb} $\leftarrow$ *\emph{h\textsubscript{2}ep-} $\to$ Sanskrit \textbf{áp-}, and the \textbf{-âb} inside \textbf{Punjab}
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \textbf{âb} against Hindi's \textbf{pānī} — two different old words, not cousins
  \item \emph{Retrieve:} \textbf{dâshtan, dâr-} — “to have,” from the chapter just closed
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Ask for water politely. (\textbf{Âb, lotfan.}) What is the \textbf{\fa{ً}} at the end of \textbf{\fa{لطفاً}} called, and where else does Persian use it? (\emph{Tanvin}; only inside a few frozen Arabic adverbs.) Is Persian \textbf{\fa{آب}} related to Hindi's \textbf{pānī}? (No — two separate old words.)

Source: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D8\%A2\%D8\%A8}{Wiktionary: \fa{آب}}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D9\%84\%D8\%B7\%D9\%81\%D8\%A7\%D9\%8B}{Wiktionary: \fa{لطفاً}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nân]{\fa{نان} — bread, and a root this track cannot trace}

\label{lesson:FA-C09-nan}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\fa{آب،} \fa{لطفاً}} (\emph{âb, lotfan}). This chapter's second request names the other thing on every Persian table.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\fa{نان}} — \emph{nân} — \textbf{bread}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\fa{نان،} \fa{لطفاً}.} — \emph{nân, lotfan.} — \textbf{Bread, please.}
\end{quote}

Three letters, all already yours: \textbf{\fa{ن} \fa{ا} \fa{ن}} — \emph{n}, long \emph{â}, \emph{n} again.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\fa{نان}} continues Middle Persian \textbf{nān}, and there this word's trail runs cold: no secure root beyond that form is agreed, and no English cousin can honestly be claimed. Not every word in this book gets a family tree, and this one is named plainly rather than forced into one.

The word travelled anyway, just not by inheritance. Persian \textbf{\fa{نان}} passed into Hindi-Urdu as \textbf{nān}, and from there into English as \textbf{naan} — the bread on a restaurant menu is this exact word, arriving by borrowing three languages after Persian, not by any shared ancestor.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{nân} — bread
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{nân, lotfan.} — bread, please
  \item \emph{Name:} the one fact this word's history gives you — Middle Persian \textbf{nān}, root beyond that unknown
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \textbf{nân} $\to$ Hindi-Urdu \textbf{nān} $\to$ English \textbf{naan} — a borrowing, not a cousin
  \item \emph{Run through:} \textbf{âb, lotfan} — \textbf{nân, lotfan} — two requests back to back
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\fa{نان}} mean? (\textbf{Bread.}) Does it have a secure Indo-European cousin? (No — the trail runs cold at Middle Persian \textbf{nān}.) Which English word is this same word, borrowed rather than inherited? (\textbf{Naan}, via Hindi-Urdu.)

Source: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D9\%86\%D8\%A7\%D9\%86}{Wiktionary: \fa{نان}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[chây]{\fa{چای} — tea, and the road that gave everyone but Europe the same word}

\label{lesson:FA-C09-chay}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\fa{نان،} \fa{لطفاً}} (\emph{nân, lotfan}). Here is the drink that usually comes with it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\fa{چای}} — \emph{chây} — \textbf{tea}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\fa{چای،} \fa{لطفاً}.} — \emph{chây, lotfan.} — \textbf{Tea, please.}
\end{quote}

Three letters, all already yours: \textbf{\fa{چ}} \emph{ch}, from \textbf{\fa{چیست}}; long \textbf{\fa{ا}} \emph{â}; \textbf{\fa{ی}} as a closing glide.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\fa{چای}} is not an inherited Persian word at all — it is a loan, and a comparatively recent one. It continues Northern Chinese \textbf{chá}, carried overland through Central Asia into Persian, the same road Russian \textbf{chai} and Turkish \textbf{çay} travelled.

The word did not stop at Persian. \textbf{\fa{چای}} itself passed onward into Urdu as \textbf{\fa{چائے}} \emph{chāy}, the same three-step road: Chinese into Persian into Urdu. Tea that instead reached Europe by \textbf{sea} carried a different, southern-Chinese form, which is why English says \textbf{tea} and French says \emph{thé} rather than \emph{chai}: one drink, two words, sorted by whether it travelled by land or by water.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{chây} — tea
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{chây, lotfan.} — tea, please
  \item \emph{Name:} the road — Chinese \textbf{chá} $\to$ Persian \textbf{chây} $\to$ Urdu \textbf{chāy}
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \textbf{chây}, which travelled by land, against \textbf{tea}, which travelled by sea
  \item \emph{Run through:} \textbf{âb, lotfan} — \textbf{nân, lotfan} — \textbf{chây, lotfan}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which language gave Persian \textbf{\fa{چای}}? (\textbf{Chinese}, overland.) Which language borrowed this exact Persian word onward? (\textbf{Urdu}, as \textbf{\fa{چائے}}.) Why does English say \textbf{tea} instead? (It arrived by sea, carrying a different Chinese form.)

Source: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%DA\%86\%D8\%A7\%DB\%8C}{Wiktionary: \fa{چای}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kelid]{\fa{کلید} — key, a Greek word Persian has held for two thousand years}

\label{lesson:FA-C09-kelid}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\fa{چای،} \fa{لطفاً}}. Then recall the small linking \emph{-e} the first sentence taught inside \textbf{\fa{اسمِ} \fa{من}} — you will need it again in a moment.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\fa{کلید}} — \emph{kelid} — \textbf{key}
\end{quote}

Four letters, all already yours: \textbf{\fa{ک}} \emph{k}, from \textbf{\fa{کمک}}; \textbf{\fa{ل}} \emph{l}; \textbf{\fa{ی}} long \emph{i}; \textbf{\fa{د}} \emph{d}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a possessive request, built from an old part}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\fa{کلیدِ} \fa{من،} \fa{لطفاً}.} — \emph{kelid-e man, lotfan.} — \textbf{My key, please.}
\end{quote}

No new grammar here — this reuses the ezafe \textbf{-e} exactly as \textbf{\fa{اسمِ} \fa{من}} did, now linking a household word to its owner instead of a name. A request can carry an owner the same way a name did.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\fa{کلید}} is not inherited Persian at all — it is a loan from Greek \textbf{kleidíon}, “little key,” one of a handful of Greek words that entered Persian in the Hellenistic centuries after Alexander's conquest, when Greek-speaking rulers governed Iranian land for generations. The parent word, \textbf{kleís}, shares its Indo-European root with Latin \emph{claudere}, “to close” — the root behind English \textbf{close}, \textbf{conclude}, and \textbf{exclude}. This chapter's four words now stand for all three of Persian's vocabulary layers: inherited \textbf{\fa{آب}}, an untraceable \textbf{\fa{نان}}, an overland Chinese loan in \textbf{\fa{چای}}, and a Greek loan in \textbf{\fa{کلید}}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{kelid} — key; then \textbf{kelid-e man, lotfan} — my key, please
  \item \emph{Connect:} \textbf{kelid} $\leftarrow$ Greek \textbf{kleidíon} $\to$ Latin \emph{claudere} $\to$ English \textbf{close}, \textbf{conclude}, \textbf{exclude}
  \item \emph{Run through:} \textbf{âb}, \textbf{nân}, \textbf{chây}, \textbf{kelid} — each with \textbf{, lotfan}
  \item \emph{Sort:} which of the four is inherited, which is untraceable, which travelled by land, which came from Greek
  \item \emph{Retrieve:} the ezafe \textbf{-e} from \textbf{\fa{اسمِ} \fa{من}}, now on \textbf{\fa{کلیدِ} \fa{من}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which language did Persian borrow \textbf{\fa{کلید}} from, and when? (Greek, after Alexander.) Say “my key, please.” (\textbf{Kelid-e man, lotfan.}) Name all four polite requests this chapter built. (\textbf{Âb, nân, chây, kelid}, each with \textbf{lotfan}.)

Source: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%DA\%A9\%D9\%84\%DB\%8C\%D8\%AF}{Wiktionary: \fa{کلید}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
